stem: A live scoreboard widget gets home_score, away_score and summary from Claude via output_config.format. One night the widget shows 31–17 for a game that ended 31–24. The JSON was perfectly valid. Which safeguard would have caught this?

options.text: Move the same fields to a strict tool so that schema compliance is enforced a second way.
options.explanation: Strict tools also guarantee shape only. The JSON here already matched the schema, and the values were still wrong.

options.text: Raise the effort level, because a valid schema with confident values signals a reliable answer.
options.explanation: Well-formed, confident output can still be wrong. Effort may help reasoning, but it doesn't verify the result.

options.text: Check the returned scores in code against the official box score before showing them.
options.explanation: Correct. Structured outputs guarantee shape, not truth. Semantic validation against a trusted source catches valid-but-wrong values.

options.text: Add "double-check the final score" to the prompt and trust the next output in full.
options.explanation: A prompt nudge may reduce errors, but it isn't a check. A high-visibility number needs verification in code.

stem: A ticket-routing service on Claude Opus 5.5 parses JSON.parse(response.content[0].text). It fails intermittently with "cannot read property text of undefined". Logs show that the failing responses begin with a thinking block. What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Check stop_reason first, then read the text block found by type instead of by its position.
options.explanation: Correct. Thinking or tool_use blocks can come before the text, so iterate the content blocks by type, and check stop_reason before trusting what you parse.

options.text: Send thinking set to disabled so that the first content block is always the text block.
options.explanation: Claude Opus 5.5 rejects disabled thinking with a 400 at every effort level. The parser should not depend on block order anyway.

options.text: Wrap the parse in try/catch and repeat the request until content[0] turns out to be text.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries waste money and latency and leave the positional assumption in place.

options.text: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening brace so that the reply starts directly with JSON.
options.explanation: Prefilling the last assistant turn returns a 400 on Claude 4.6 and later models.

stem: A fantasy trade analyzer uses output_config.format with a JSON schema, and the team assumes that every response will now parse. In which situations can the response still fail to match the schema? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The response is streamed to the client instead of being returned in one piece.
options.explanation: Structured outputs work with streaming. The finished output still follows the schema.

options.text: The response stops with stop_reason "max_tokens" before the JSON is complete.
options.explanation: Correct. Truncated output can be incomplete and invalid. Retry with a higher max_tokens.

options.text: The same schema was already compiled and cached by an earlier request that day.
options.explanation: Grammar caching only removes the compile latency. It doesn't weaken the constraint.

options.text: The input prompt is very long, for example a full season of game logs.
options.explanation: Input length doesn't relax the output constraint. Long inputs are not one of the documented exceptions.

options.text: The response stops with stop_reason "refusal" and returns HTTP 200.
options.explanation: Correct. A refusal takes precedence over the schema, so the output may not match it even though the call succeeded.

stem: A support triage schema has a priority enum of "Needs review", "High priority" and "Low priority". The output always parses, yet a downstream switch statement occasionally falls through because Claude returned "High Priority". What is the best fix?

options.text: Add "copy enum values with exact capitalization" in capitals to the system prompt.
options.explanation: A prompt rule may reduce how often it happens, but casing isn't guaranteed. The consumer still has to tolerate it.

options.text: Switch the extraction to a strict tool, which enforces exact enum casing.
options.explanation: The casing caveat applies to strict tool use as well as JSON outputs.

options.text: Set additionalProperties to false on the schema so that no other values are allowed.
options.explanation: additionalProperties controls extra keys on objects, not the capitalization of enum strings.

options.text: Compare enum values case-insensitively, and avoid values that differ only in case.
options.explanation: Correct. Structured outputs don't guarantee enum capitalization, so the consumer should normalize case.

stem: A developer adds "minimum": 0 and "maximum": 1 to a confidence field in a raw JSON schema sent in output_config.format, and the request now fails with a 400. The application still needs the 0–1 range enforced. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Send the schema through the deprecated output_format parameter, which accepted those constraints.
options.explanation: output_format is deprecated and the schema limitations are the same. It doesn't add support for numerical constraints.

options.text: Use an SDK schema helper that strips the bounds from the sent schema and validates them on the response.
options.explanation: Correct. Validating SDK helpers remove unsupported constraints from what is sent, note them in the field description, and check the result against the original constraints.

options.text: Delete the bounds and rely on the description "a number from 0 to 1" without checking it.
options.explanation: Removing the bounds fixes the 400, but leaves the range unenforced. Something still has to validate it.

options.text: Enable citations on the input documents, so Claude grounds the confidence value in the source.
options.explanation: Citations are incompatible with output_config.format (a 400), and they don't enforce a numeric range.

stem: An injury-report summarizer sometimes states that a player has been "cleared for contact" when the team's report says nothing of the kind. The summaries read fluently and confidently. Which prompt change best reduces these unsupported claims?

options.text: Ask Claude to use a more cautious tone throughout so readers know to double-check it.
options.explanation: A softer tone hides the problem instead of removing it. The unsupported claim is still there.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so Claude has enough room to describe every player completely.
options.explanation: Output length has nothing to do with whether claims are grounded in the source.

options.text: Switch to structured outputs so that each player's status is a validated field.
options.explanation: A schema guarantees shape, not truth. A wrong status still fits the field.

options.text: Require a supporting quote from the report for each claim, allowing "not stated".
options.explanation: Correct. Grounding claims in direct quotes, removing any claim without one, and allowing Claude to say it doesn't know all reduce hallucinations.

stem: A draft-trade evaluator validates Claude's JSON with Zod, and about 2% of responses fail validation. Today the service retries every failure in a loop until it passes. Which changes make the pipeline more robust? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Check stop_reason before parsing, and retry max_tokens stops with a higher limit.
options.explanation: Correct. Truncation is a common cause of invalid JSON, and it needs more room rather than the same request again.

options.text: Fill any field that fails validation with a default value and pass the record on.
options.explanation: Silently inventing values hides failures and puts fabricated data into downstream decisions.

options.text: Prefill the assistant turn with the start of the JSON object to keep it on track.
options.explanation: Prefill returns a 400 on current models. Use structured outputs to constrain the shape.

options.text: Raise the retry limit so that the loop keeps going until every response passes.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries cost money and can loop forever on an input that will never pass.

options.text: Retry with the validation error included a bounded number of times, then flag it.
options.explanation: Correct. Feeding back the specific error helps Claude correct it, and a cap with escalation keeps failures visible.

stem: A CRM import job writes Claude's structured output to CSV by taking the values in the order they appear. Its schema lists notes, name, email and age, with only name and email required. The notes column keeps receiving names. What is the best fix?

options.text: Map each value by its key name, or mark every property as required.
options.explanation: Correct. Structured outputs place required properties first, then optional ones. Reading by key, or making all properties required, removes the dependence on position.

options.text: Tell Claude in the prompt to keep the property order of the schema.
options.explanation: Structured outputs always emit required properties before optional ones, whatever the prompt says. Positional parsing stays fragile.

options.text: Prefill the response with the notes key so that it is emitted first.
options.explanation: Prefill is incompatible with JSON outputs and returns a 400 on current models.

options.text: Turn on citations so that every value is linked back to its field.
options.explanation: Citations can't be combined with output_config.format, and they don't control property order.

stem: A rules-desk tool sends the league rulebook as a document with `citations: {enabled: true}` and also sets `output_config.format` so the answer comes back as JSON. Every request now fails with a 400. Officials need both a cited answer and machine-readable fields. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Switch from `output_config.format` to the older `output_format` parameter, which works with citations
options.explanation: `output_format` is deprecated and is still structured outputs, so it doesn't remove the conflict.

options.text: Get the cited answer first, then turn it into JSON in a separate structured-output call
options.explanation: Correct. Citations and structured outputs can't be combined in one request. Splitting the work keeps the citations and still produces validated JSON.

options.text: Keep both features and retry the request, since the 400 is a temporary validation error
options.explanation: A 400 fails the same way every time. The two features are incompatible, so retrying can't succeed.

options.text: Drop citations and ask Claude to paste rulebook passages into a JSON field instead
options.explanation: Pasted quotes aren't verified citations, so officials lose the guarantee that the cited text really comes from the document.

stem: An agent's `update_depth_chart` tool sometimes receives calls with a missing `player_id` or with extra fields the handler doesn't expect, and the handler crashes. The team wants the tool arguments to match the schema every time. Which change best fits?

options.text: Repeat the parameter list in the tool description in capital letters
options.explanation: Stronger wording may help, but it's still a request. It doesn't guarantee that the arguments match the schema.

options.text: Wrap the handler in a try/except and silently skip calls that crash
options.explanation: This hides the failures and drops depth-chart updates without telling anyone.

options.text: Ask Claude for the arguments as free text and parse them with a regular expression instead
options.explanation: Free text is less constrained than a tool schema, so this makes mismatches more likely.

options.text: Set `strict: true` on the tool, with `required` and `additionalProperties: false`
options.explanation: Correct. Strict tool use constrains the tool input to the schema, so required fields are present and unexpected ones are excluded.

stem: A roster bot decides which team a tool call refers to by checking whether the serialized tool input string contains `"team":"KC"`. After a model upgrade, the check starts missing calls that clearly target that team, although the tool inputs look correct when logged. What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Add more string patterns that cover spaces and different quote styles
options.explanation: This chases one serialization detail after another. The next change in escaping breaks it again.

options.text: Pin the old model permanently so the input string keeps its previous format
options.explanation: This postpones the problem until that model is retired and blocks every other upgrade.

options.text: Parse the tool input as JSON and compare the `team` field's value
options.explanation: Correct. Different models can escape JSON strings differently. Parsing the input and reading the field is independent of serialization details.

options.text: Ask Claude in the system prompt to always format tool inputs without spaces
options.explanation: This depends on the model's formatting habits instead of fixing a fragile parser.

stem: A replay-review assistant asks Claude to put its ruling inside `<verdict>` tags, and the parser requires the entire response to match `^<verdict>(.*)</verdict>$`. Parsing fails whenever Claude adds a short sentence before the tags, although the verdict itself is correct. Which change best fits?

options.text: Extract the `<verdict>` content wherever it appears, ignoring surrounding text
options.explanation: Correct. Tag-based extraction should find the tagged part and ignore surrounding text. If an exact shape is truly required, structured outputs is the stronger tool.

options.text: Retry the request until the response contains nothing but the tags
options.explanation: Retrying discards correct verdicts and adds cost and latency to fix a parser problem.

options.text: Prefill the assistant turn with `<verdict>` so Claude can't write anything before it
options.explanation: Assistant prefill is rejected on current models, so this request would fail with a 400.

options.text: Treat any response that fails the match as an "inconclusive" ruling
options.explanation: This turns correct verdicts into wrong outcomes just because of extra text.
